Convalescent Plasma Therapy

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
..... a promising treatment for Covid-19

Unique Selling Point:
This could be a game changer in the fight against the virus.

Summary:
Blood from COVID-19 survivors can be a rich source of antibodies or proteins that the immune system makes to attack the SARS-CoV-2 virus, the virus causing COVID-19. Plasma is the part of the blood that contains these valuable antibodies. It has long been the focus of treatment during pandemics and it is surmised that if you give somebody who is really sick a dose of somebody else’s antibodies that it will assist in their recovery.

The method has been used during the 1918 Spanish Flu and also for Ebola treatments. There are currently dozens of studies underway across the globe looking at this as a treat possible treatment for Covid. Some results are trickling in and it seems positive.

The Mayo Clinic has determined that giving sick Covid patients plasma does not harms them, and seems to have positive effects.

Another study from Methodist Hospital in Houston shows a 75% success rate. However, the Houston study was a small one. But it is very encouraging.

In the US , the US National COVID-19 Convalescent Plasma Project, a group of physicians and scientists from 57 institutions in 46 states are involved in clinical trials.

Here in South Africa people who have recovered from COVID-19 are donating their blood to help others who are trying to fight off the disease. It is part of a South African clinical trial involving 600 volunteers and is headed by the SA National Blood Service.


Further information:
Blood from COVID-19 survivors can be a rich source of antibodies or proteins that the immune system makes to attack the SARS-CoV-2 virus, the virus causing COVID-19. Plasma is the part of the blood that contains these valuable antibodies. It has long been the focus of treatment during pandemics and it is surmised that if you give somebody who is really sick a dose of somebody else’s antibodies that it will assist in their recovery. This isn’t a new treatment; it was used to treat diphtheria in the 1890s and used — effectively — during the 1918 flu pandemic. Plasma infusions also have been used to treat people with diseases like SARS, measles, and chickenpox.

With COVID-19, some early information suggests plasma infusions have helped some patients’ recovery time, but it’s still too early to tell how effective the treatment is.
To determine scientifically of the treatment is effective, there are currently dozens of studies underway across the globe looking at this as a possible treatment for Covid.

• In the US, the US National COVID-19 Convalescent Plasma Project, a group of physicians and scientists from 57 institutions in 46 states are involved in clinical trials.

• In the UK the University of Oxford is busy with a large clinical trial. More than 6,500 people registered their interest for the plasma donation programme, which is being led by NHS Blood and Transplant on behalf of the government. The organisation is recruiting people with the help of NHS data and inviting suitable candidates who have recovered from a confirmed case of coronavirus or had symptoms to donate plasma at its 23 main blood centres.

• Here in South Africa people who have recovered from COVID-19 are donating their blood to help others who are trying to fight off the disease. It is part of a South African clinical trial involving 600 volunteers and is headed by the SA National Blood Service.

Over the last 3 months a lot of research has been done, and some results are trickling in.

• The Mayo Clinic has determined that giving sick Covid patients plasma does not harm them at all, and seems to have positive effects. See https://eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2020-06/mc-mfc061820.php. Recent Tweet: “This diverse study lead by @DrMJoyner, an anaesthesiologist at Mayo Clinic, found that convalescent plasma treatment was safe, inexpensive, and the mortality rates in sick patients were quite low. #COVID19 @Carolynyjohnson via @washingtonpost”. Mayo Clinic researchers and collaborators have found investigational convalescent plasma to be safe following transfusion in a diverse group of 20,000 patients. The findings -- from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's Expanded Access Program for COVID-19 -- are reported in Mayo Clinic Proceedings.

• The US’ first convalescent plasma transfusion trial results have been peer-reviewed and published, showing 19 out of 25 patients improving with the treatment and 11 discharged from the hospital. On March 28, Houston Methodist became the first academic medical center in the nation to transfuse plasma from recovered COVID-19 patients into two critically ill patients. With no adverse side effects caused by the plasma transfusion, the study concluded that convalescent plasma is a safe treatment option for patients with severe COVID-19 disease. To date, this is the largest cohort worldwide assessed for outcomes pertaining to convalescent plasma transfusion for COVID-19. The findings are described in a paper appearing in press May 26 (online May 28) in The American Journal of Pathology. This is the first peer-reviewed publication on convalescent plasma use in the U.S.A.

So, while the Houston study is very promising, it was conducted on a small number of patients – it is, therefore, imperative to continue with larger studies, such as the one in South Africa.

Layers in the story:
• Therapeutic vs vaccine
• What are antibodies and long do they last?
• What is immunity and how is it reached?
• There is a company in the US that is attempting to bio-engineer antibodies and seem to have had some success. The company is called Centivax or Distributedbio:
https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20200518005767/en/Centivax-Antibodies-Neutralize-Pandemic-Coronavirus-Independently-Confirmed

Potential interviewees:
• Dr Marion Vermeulen, a SANBS biomedical scientist who is also co-principal investigator for the South African trial.

• Dr James Musser, Professor of pathology and genomic medicine with the Houston Methodist Research Institute, is the principal investigator who led the project to treat critically ill COVID-19 patients with convalescent plasma.

• Dr Devorah Wineberg, donating plasma and antibodies

• Dr Jacob Glanville, CEO of Distributed Bio and Centivax. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EvfulLdrND0

Script:


V/O:
This is Dr Devorah Wineberg, a medical doctor who has recovered from Covid-19. She is at a National Blood Service facility, and the machine she is linked to is extracting the portion of her blood called plasma. Her fight with the virus has altered her blood plasma in such a way that it could now be a powerful medicine to help others infected with the Coronavirus.

This is possible because of the way the Coronavirus infects people, says Dr Jake Glanville a bioengineer in San Francisco.
Glanville:
So if you were to Zoom into the Coronavirus with a very powerful microscope you would see that it is surrounded by a series of vicious looking spikes and at the tip of those spikes it has something called the receptor binding domain, and its job is to bind to a specific receptor on human cells.
V/O:
The virus binds to the receptor and then uses that as a key to gain access to the cell. The human body responds to this attack by producing antibodies.
Glanville:
What antibodies do is they go and they block those spikes, so they cap them so that the virus is no longer able to infect your cells. We call this neutralizing the virus.
V/O:
And these protective antibodies lurk in blood plasma, the liquid portion of blood that carries blood cells and proteins throughout the body. It is fairly easy to separate blood cells from plasma.
LINK:
In this vial the plasma and the red blood cells have been separated. The plasma on top and the red blood cells at the bottom.
V/O:
If somebody has successfully recovered from a viral infection, their plasma is rich in the antibodies that defeated the virus. This plasma is called convalescent plasma.

Somebody who becomes really sick from a viral infection, does not produce effective or enough antibodies to fight off the virus. However, if they could get access to large quantities of antibodies, it could help them to defeat the virus, and recover.

So, for a long time doctors have been experimenting with giving patients convalescent plasma, rich in antibodies as a therapy to treat viral infections. .

At the Methodist Hospital in Houston Dr James Musser is one of the leading experts on convalescent plasma therapy for Covid patients.
Musser:
Yes, convalescent plasma plasma therapy is turning out to be a very very important of our fight against the Cornonavirus, here in the United States and other countries
V/O:
Here in South Africa, the South African National Blood Service has also launched a clinical trial exploring convalescent plasma therapy. Marion Vermeulen is the Senior Manager for Operations Testing at the SANBS.
Derek:
How will this study fit into international trials around the word?

Marion:
So there’s many countries doing trials exactly like this and they are all slightly different. Europe have been doing trials like this, the UK, America have done a number of trials as well. China also did some trials and unfortunately some of these trials had to end because they can’t enrol enough people because they have come near the end of their pandemic. So we are in the perfect time now where we are in the spike of this pandemic actually.
V/O:
However, as no formal clinical trials have previously been done to scientifically determine the efficacy and safety of coronavirus convalescent plasma therapies, it has made some researchers hesitant to start using it.
Derek:
Doctor, there are some scientists who say it is not safe?
Musser:
No. In many of the studies that have now been published in peer reviewed journals it has been proven to be safe. There is no question about the safety. We had the first paper that was in a peer reviewed journal that showed in a small number of patients that it was safe. More recently a very large study, spearheaded by the Mayo group in well over 5000 patients similarly showed that it is a safe therapy to give to patients.
LINK:
Convalescent plasma therapy should not be confused with vaccination. They are completely different.
Glanville:
With a vaccine you inject little pieces of the virus and that person’s own immune system over the next 8 weeks learns how to make antibodies and those antibodies block the virus. What we are doing is that instead of injecting pieces of the virus, we are skipping that whole process. We are just injecting antibodies, so immediately it is in their body. If they get exposed to the virus the antibodies will surround it, block it up and stop it from infecting cells.

The advantage of this approach is that every nation in the world currently has that medicine available, because every nation in the world has recovered patients.
LINK:
Convalescent plasma therapy is nothing new. It was first used more than a hundred years ago.
Marion:
Convalescent plasma has been around since 1918. It was first used in the Spanish flu and quite successfully. It is the fastest treatment when there is no other treatment available. It is very easy to produce and to be able to do. It was also used in SARS 1 and also in MERS very successfully.
V/O:
And now it is also used in the fight against Covid-19 with very promising results.
Musser:
One of the important findings in our study is that it looks like the earlier in the course of hospitalization that you give the plasma the better that works in helping patients. And we are giving what we call high titer plasma which simply means that it has a high concentration of antibodies directed against the corona virus.
LINK:
Despite the fact that the benefits of plasma therapy are still being investigated a large number of patients in the United States are already receiving the treatment.
Musser:
Herein the US there have been over 60 000. Six zero thousand patients who have received convalescent therapy with convalescent plasma. So is has become a very important part of our fight against Conornavirus here in the US.
V/O:
However, many of these treatments do not from part of clinical trials so the efficacy of these interventions cannot be verified scientifically.
Link:
The South African Study is underway and convalescent plasma has been collected for some time now.
Marion:
So far we have sixty donors who have enrolled into the programme and we have collected fifty units of blood at this point.
V/O:
People who have recovered from Covid-19 can begin to donate antibodies 28 days after their last symptoms.
Derek:
How often can you donate?
Devorha:
So according to the guideline of the SANBS, they bring me back every two weeks.
V/O:
So, in the first stage of the clinical trial plasma is harvested. The next phase will only start once enough plasma has been collected. The patients will then be infused with the convalescent antibodies.

Donating plasma is a simple process, and very similar to donating blood.
Marion:
Normally when you donate blood the needle goes into your arm, you go straight into the bag and the whole blood is collected. For this procedure we are only collecting the plasma. Si it is very similar to anyone who has ever done platelet donation, it is called plasmapheresis. You connect it to an instrument and that instrument has a centrifuge in it, so the whole blood comes out, it is centrifuged, and the red cells are given back to you. We only collect the plasma component of the blood.
V/O:
So, worldwide convalescent plasma is seen by many researchers as a potential life-saving therapy. However, bioengineers have now taken antibody therapy against Covid 19 a step further, and this could be a real game changer.

They have begun to bioengineer or create Covid antibodies in the lab. These antibodies are called monoclonal antibodies because they are clones of a specific antibody, tailor-made to neutralise the Coronavirus.
Glanville:
Now we have it manufacturing, and the idea is that in an antibody therapeutic you can produce and endless supply in these large bio-vats. They look like beer fermentation tanks, except we are growing antibodies instead of instead of delicious beer.
V/O:
And a limitless supply of antibodies could mean that Covid-19 patients’ immune systems could be flooded with large volumes of antibodies and heal them.
Glanville:
The minute that we have an effective medicine in hospital, the whole crisis becomes less scary. If you knew that if you got sick you could go to a hospital, get an IV, feel better and go home, then the crisis is over.
V/O:
And with several promising vaccines on the horizon, Glanville is quite upbeat about the future.
Glanville:
And so, we want both of these things. We want the large-scale prevention, but we also want the effective treatment and that could put us in a position of having life return relatively to normal by the summer of 2021.
V/O:
But while effective vaccines and a limitless supply of engineered antibodies are still in the future, the South African study on convalescent plasma therapy remains crucial in the current fight against the virus.
Derek:
And the study needs more donors
Devorah:
Yes, it does net more donors, and we know South Africa has had lots and lots of infections so there are many people who have recovered, and I think whoever has recovered and is capable and well enough to be a donor I would strongly encourage them to come and donate.

Marion: Normally when you donate blood the needle goes into your arm, you go straight into the bag and the whole blood is collected. For this procedure we are only collecting the plasma. Si it is very similar to anyone who has ever done platelet donation, it is called plasmapheresis. You connect it to an instrument and that instrument has a centrifuge in it, so the whole blood comes out, it is centrifuged, and the red cells are given back to you. We only collect the plasma component of the blood. V/O: So, worldwide convalescent plasma is seen by many researchers as a potential life-saving therapy. However, bioengineers have now taken antibody therapy against Covid 19 a step further, and this could be a real game changer. They have begun to bioengineer or create Covid antibodies in the lab. These antibodies are called monoclonal antibodies because they are clones of a specific antibody, tailor-made to neutralise the Coronavirus. Glanville: Now we have it manufacturing, and the idea is that in an antibody therapeutic you can produce and endless supply in these large bio-vats. They look like beer fermentation tanks, except we are growing antibodies instead of instead of delicious beer. V/O: And a limitless supply of antibodies could mean that Covid-19 patients’ immune systems could be flooded with large volumes of antibodies and heal them. Glanville: The minute that we have an effective medicine in hospital, the whole crisis becomes less scary. If you knew that if you got sick you could go to a hospital, get an IV, feel better and go home, then the crisis is over. V/O: And with several promising vaccines on the horizon, Glanville is quite upbeat about the future. Glanville: And so, we want both of these things. We want the large-scale prevention, but we also want the effective treatment and that could put us in a position of having life return relatively to normal by the summer of 2021. V/O: But while effective vaccines and a limitless supply of engineered antibodies are still in the future, the South African study on convalescent plasma therapy remains crucial in the current fight against the virus. Derek: And the study needs more donors Devorah: Yes, it does net more donors, and we know South Africa has had lots and lots of infections so there are many people who have recovered, and I think whoever has recovered and is capable and well enough to be a donor I would strongly encourage them to come and donate.

metadata.Further information: Blood from COVID-19 survivors can be a rich source of antibodies or proteins that the immune system makes to attack the SARS-CoV-2 virus, the virus causing COVID-19. Plasma is the part of the blood that contains these valuable antibodies. It has long been the focus of treatment during pandemics and it is surmised that if you give somebody who is really sick a dose of somebody else’s antibodies that it will assist in their recovery. This isn’t a new treatment; it was used to treat diphtheria in the 1890s and used — effectively — during the 1918 flu pandemic. Plasma infusions also have been used to treat people with diseases like SARS, measles, and chickenpox. With COVID-19, some early information suggests plasma infusions have helped some patients’ recovery time, but it’s still too early to tell how effective the treatment is. To determine scientifically of the treatment is effective, there are currently dozens of studies underway across the globe looking at this as a possible treatment for Covid. • In the US, the US National COVID-19 Convalescent Plasma Project, a group of physicians and scientists from 57 institutions in 46 states are involved in clinical trials. • In the UK the University of Oxford is busy with a large clinical trial. More than 6,500 people registered their interest for the plasma donation programme, which is being led by NHS Blood and Transplant on behalf of the government. The organisation is recruiting people with the help of NHS data and inviting suitable candidates who have recovered from a confirmed case of coronavirus or had symptoms to donate plasma at its 23 main blood centres. • Here in South Africa people who have recovered from COVID-19 are donating their blood to help others who are trying to fight off the disease. It is part of a South African clinical trial involving 600 volunteers and is headed by the SA National Blood Service. Over the last 3 months a lot of research has been done, and some results are trickling in. • The Mayo Clinic has determined that giving sick Covid patients plasma does not harm them at all, and seems to have positive effects. See https://eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2020-06/mc-mfc061820.php. Recent Tweet: “This diverse study lead by @DrMJoyner, an anaesthesiologist at Mayo Clinic, found that convalescent plasma treatment was safe, inexpensive, and the mortality rates in sick patients were quite low. #COVID19 @Carolynyjohnson via @washingtonpost”. Mayo Clinic researchers and collaborators have found investigational convalescent plasma to be safe following transfusion in a diverse group of 20,000 patients. The findings -- from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's Expanded Access Program for COVID-19 -- are reported in Mayo Clinic Proceedings. • The US’ first convalescent plasma transfusion trial results have been peer-reviewed and published, showing 19 out of 25 patients improving with the treatment and 11 discharged from the hospital. On March 28, Houston Methodist became the first academic medical center in the nation to transfuse plasma from recovered COVID-19 patients into two critically ill patients. With no adverse side effects caused by the plasma transfusion, the study concluded that convalescent plasma is a safe treatment option for patients with severe COVID-19 disease. To date, this is the largest cohort worldwide assessed for outcomes pertaining to convalescent plasma transfusion for COVID-19. The findings are described in a paper appearing in press May 26 (online May 28) in The American Journal of Pathology. This is the first peer-reviewed publication on convalescent plasma use in the U.S.A. So, while the Houston study is very promising, it was conducted on a small number of patients – it is, therefore, imperative to continue with larger studies, such as the one in South Africa. Layers in the story: • Therapeutic vs vaccine • What are antibodies and long do they last? • What is immunity and how is it reached? • There is a company in the US that is attempting to bio-engineer antibodies and seem to have had some success. The company is called Centivax or Distributedbio: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20200518005767/en/Centivax-Antibodies-Neutralize-Pandemic-Coronavirus-Independently-Confirmed Potential interviewees: • Dr Marion Vermeulen, a SANBS biomedical scientist who is also co-principal investigator for the South African trial. • Dr James Musser, Professor of pathology and genomic medicine with the Houston Methodist Research Institute, is the principal investigator who led the project to treat critically ill COVID-19 patients with convalescent plasma. • Dr Devorah Wineberg, donating plasma and antibodies • Dr Jacob Glanville, CEO of Distributed Bio and Centivax. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EvfulLdrND0
